summary: In the spring of 1868 the summer-house at Windygates had been home to a pair of owls, but by that autumn it was full of ladies and gentlemen at a lawn party given by the new tenant. The women's bright summer dresses stood out against the men's dull clothes, and through the arches a green lawn stretched toward flower-beds, trees and a large stone house with a fountain. While the guests were talking and laughing loudly, one shrill voice called for silence. A young lady then stepped out in front of the summer-house and looked over the crowd like a general reviewing troops. She was young, pretty, plump and fair, completely at ease, and dressed in the height of fashion, from her tilted flat hat and piled-up hair to her striped stockings and very high heels.

Sir Patrick opened a snuff-box hidden in the knob of his ivory cane, took a pinch, and chuckled at a private thought. He told Arnold that he really was a stranger at the house, since he and Lady Lundie wrote to each other on good terms but met as rarely as possible. He explained that his story was a bit like Arnold's, because he had been earning his living as a Scottish lawyer when his brother remarried and then died without a son, which made him the baronet. He said he regretted the title, because it loaded him with responsibilities, including being head of the family and his niece's guardian, and forced him to attend this lawn party. Feeling out of place and seeing no familiar faces, he asked Arnold whether he knew anyone there.

Miss Silvester listed Delamayn's advantages: he was a nobleman's son, handsome, popular at college and welcome in the best houses in England. She then asked whether he was also a coward and a scoundrel. He started, nearly answered, and then tried uneasily to laugh it off, telling her to keep her temper. She scornfully asked whether he of all men expected her to stay calm, and reminded him of the time when she had foolishly believed he loved her and would keep his promise. Still trying to laugh, he said that mad was a rather strong word for her to use.

She told him that even if the landlady doubted her story, he only had to arrive and ask for his wife to prove it true. She said her part, being alone with the suspicious woman, was the hard one, and asked whether he would do his. Unable to refuse outright, he dodged by saying he did not know how they were to be married. She replied that he did know, since in Scotland there were no forms, ceremonies or delays, and a couple only needed witnesses to be married. Her plan would get her into the inn and let him join her naturally, and whatever the landlady thought of the deception afterward, they would have achieved their aim without any risk to him.

Arnold said he had always thought it was moist sugar, and Sir Patrick surprised him by urging him to marry, saying he was one of the few men with a fair chance of success. Settling in for a talk, Sir Patrick explained that the moist sugar bought at a tea-shop is really a mixture of adulterations made to look like sugar, which people swallow anyway by ignoring the fact. Arnold, though really confused, said he followed. Sir Patrick went on that a man gets a wife at the marriage-shop believing she has lovely yellow hair, a fine complexion, a plump figure and good height, only to find the hair dyed, the skin powdered, the plumpness padding and three inches of height in her heels. If a man can shut his eyes and accept such a wife as he accepts adulterated sugar, Sir Patrick concluded, he has a fair chance of a successful marriage.

Arnold's friend refused to put the woman first, saying he would not risk being cut out of his father's will for any woman. Arnold had long admired him as a great athlete, especially as a swimmer, and this answer shook his faith in him, though only for a moment. Arnold coldly said his friend knew best and asked what he could do. The friend asked him to go and tell her what had happened, proposing that they leave as if both heading for the railway and that he drop Arnold at the foot-path in the gig. He assured Arnold that he could catch the evening train home afterward, that it was a kindness to an old friend, and that there was no risk of discovery since he would drive and no servant would come with them.

Lady Lundie was taken aback when Hester Dethridge gave an affirmative answer, and at first thought the cook must have misunderstood. She realized that Blanche, her step-daughter, was as determined to trace Anne Silvester as she was, and might stand in her way. Deeply offended by the way Anne had left the house, the vindictive Lady Lundie had planned to uncover anything compromising in the governess's secret and spread it among her friends, which would be impossible with Blanche openly on Anne's side. She rang twice for her own maid and then turned to the cook, who was still waiting calmly with her slate in hand. Lady Lundie sternly told her she had done wrong and was bound to answer her mistress, but the cook interrupted with a bow, which Lady Lundie resented.

Miss Silvester winced as she began to understand what Arnold meant. He hesitated, not wanting to hurt her, and asked her not to be angry, explaining that he and Geoffrey were old friends and Geoffrey trusted him. She stopped him and, speaking to herself, recalled that when she had asked whether Geoffrey was there, this man had answered for him. With a cry of horror she pushed away the letter Arnold offered and accused him of not looking at her, realizing that Geoffrey had told him everything. Arnold kept urging her to read Geoffrey's letter, if not in fairness to him then in fairness to Geoffrey.

Bishopriggs suddenly came in with the dinner, and Anne nervously moved away from Arnold. Watching her with his one good eye, he insisted he had warned them he could not knock this time and should not be blamed. He then moved her chair back, saying it went against all the customs of a honeymoon to sit so far from her husband. Arnold told her to let the man have his way, and Anne replied that he should get it over quickly because she could not bear it much longer. Uncovering a fried trout, Bishopriggs remarked that it had been leaping in the water half an hour earlier and called it an emblem of human life for them to think about.

After Sir Patrick left abruptly, Anne bitterly remarked on how society showed its sympathy to a friendless woman. Her irritation soon passed, as she saw that he had left to spare her from explaining her situation at the inn and to let her decide how to help him keep the peace at Windygates. Knowing she could do nothing with Lady Lundie but had great influence over Blanche, she sat down at a side-table to write to Blanche and prevent the clash Sir Patrick feared. In the letter she promised to reassure Blanche soon and begged her not to argue with Lady Lundie about her and not to come to see her. She stopped, tearful at the thought that she should dread seeing her darling Blanche, then sighed and went on writing.

Bishopriggs reasoned that a letter he had found might matter in the future, so, using the business habits he had picked up as a clerk in Sir Patrick's chambers, he wrote on it a dated note of how he had found it. He decided to keep it, hoping a reward might one day be offered, perhaps worth five pounds. Meanwhile Arnold had finished dinner, pulled a table up to the sofa where Anne lay, and pressed her to play a game of ecarte to take her mind off the storm. Too tired to argue, she agreed, thinking that nothing could make things worse and that she should not burden this kind-hearted young man with her misery. They were terrible players, and the game began with Anne turning up the nine of diamonds as trump and Arnold cheerfully predicting his own defeat before leading the queen of trumps.

Lady Lundie's maid explained that her mistress had guessed why Blanche left suddenly in the pony-chaise and meant to follow her, but an attack of giddiness brought on by the day's stress forced her to send the maid instead. The maid had brought a change of clothes because of the weather and said she was authorized to go on to the shooting-cottage and hand the matter to Sir Patrick if needed, leaving Blanche to decide whether to go back. Blanche said she would return to Windygates and face a scolding, which did not worry her, but she was anxious about Anne and asked whether Anne would stay at the inn. Since Geoffrey had promised to write to her there, Anne said she would remain for now. Blanche arranged that they could meet secretly at Windygates by coming through the shrubbery to the library window at lunchtime, said she would wait there ten minutes every day, made Anne promise to write, and asked if there was anything else to plan.

Julius told a waiter he had expected to meet someone at the hotel by appointment. The astonished waiter asked whether he had not heard the news and declared that the great foot-race at Fulham was ruined because Tinkler had gone stale. Not understanding, Julius sensibly said nothing and took the waiter's newspaper to work out whether Tinkler was a man and what going stale meant. The news was easy to find, printed in huge type and followed by conflicting personal accounts of the facts, with more promised in later editions. The papers announced Tinkler's staleness with great fanfare to a nation devoted to betting.

Blanche told Arnold not to sit far away, because her attention wandered unless she could look at people while they read to her. Arnold sat on a stool at her feet and began reading the first book of Paradise Lost. As a reader he cared only for sound, racing to the end of each line and stopping firmly there. Blanche called the opening beautiful, regretted never having read the Milton in the library, and proposed regular Mornings with Milton, joking that they were young enough to finish him. Then, looking at him again, she remarked that he did not seem to have come back to Windygates in good spirits.

Geoffrey told the people around him that they were all wrong and Sir Patrick was right. Without another word to them, he walked up to Sir Patrick's armchair, while his admirers followed in astonishment. He agreed with Sir Patrick that he would not take his degree and that neither he nor his friends could read, write and do sums correctly if tested. He also granted that Sir Patrick might be right that men like them could start with rowing and running and end by committing every crime, murder included, since no one knows what he may end up doing. Turning on the stunned group behind him, he told them that this was what he thought, in plain words.
